Phase 1 · Antiquity, Ancient Ritual & Sacred Proxies22

c. 70,000 BCE – 1605 · Before mass media, the bond is made by ritual, recitation, the image and the tomb.

c. 70,000 BCE The dead kept in the cave Myth & Legend · Pre-Modern · Phase 1 Neanderthals repeatedly carried their dead into one cave in northern Iraq and put them down in the floor. Shanidar 4 was found on his side with his arm under his head; Shanidar Z lay in a hollow gouged out to fit her, with a stone under her head. c. 70,000 BCE · Myth & Legend

Close ×

The dead kept in the cave

Neanderthals repeatedly carried their dead into one cave in northern Iraq and put them down in the floor. Shanidar 4 was found on his side with his arm under his head; Shanidar Z lay in a hollow gouged out to fit her, with a stone under her head. The cluster dates to roughly seventy to seventy-five thousand years ago.

The oldest evidence on this site of people treating the dead as somewhere you go, rather than something you leave behind. It sits about fifty-five thousand years before the dog, which settles an argument this site was getting wrong: one-sided attachment to a non-human does not begin with a domesticated animal. It is also the discipline case. The famous flowers were a mistake - the pollen turned out to come from burrowing rodents - and the burials survived the debunk anyway. That is what a real claim looks like after someone has been wrong about part of it. One limit worth stating: Sunghir, later and better studied, shows this was not a single uniform practice, so what Shanidar documents is the earliest instance of something that varied a great deal.

c. 40,000 BCE · Myth & Legend

Close ×

The carved animals

Upper Paleolithic carvers in Europe made small figures of animals and people from mammoth ivory from about forty thousand years ago. The Vogelherd set includes a cave lion, a bison, a horse, a bear, a mammoth, and a lion-man - a body with a human face on a lion's. At La Madeleine in France a bison carved from antler is caught mid-grooming, turning its head to lick its own side.

This is what the dog entry used to deny. Animals carrying human qualities were being made, kept and shown to other people tens of thousands of years before the dog: the grooming gesture is specifically human, and somebody carved it in antler on purpose. It also puts an anthropomorphised animal on the same taxonomy shelf as the dog roughly twenty-five thousand years ahead of it, which is the honest shape of the argument. The dog is not the first animal to be given human shape in the imagination. It is the first animal to be bred into living alongside us.

c. 9500 BCE · Myth & Legend

Close ×

Eleven thousand years of pillars

Round enclosures on a hillside in Anatolia holding T-shaped pillars carved to suggest human figures, built by people who had not yet domesticated a single animal - used for over a thousand years, then deliberately filled in and built over.

The oldest thing on this site with a claim to be about figures, and the interpretation is genuinely open, which is the point. What is not in dispute: hunter-gatherers cut limestone into anthropomorphic forms with stone and bone tools, set them upright in circles, carved them with foxes, scorpions, lions and vultures, returned to them for fourteen hundred years, and then filled the enclosures in on purpose. There is no hearth, no rubbish pit and no sign that anyone lived there - people travelled to the place. UNESCO's own nomination describes the pillars as believed to represent 'ancestors, perhaps even incipient deities', and other readings have them as totemic or protective figures. Nobody has settled it, and the carvings include a great many frightening animals: the dominant imagery is not a kind face but lions, spiders, snakes and scorpions. What this site can claim is narrow and still large: for at least a millennium, people made representations of beings, went out of their way to be near them, and eventually chose to close the place where they stood. Whether the beings were ancestors is the question this entry cannot answer, and saying so is more useful here than guessing.

c. 3000 BCE · Myth & Legend

Close ×

The ka statue and the false door

Egyptian tombs included a false door and a statue of the deceased, a physical seat for the ka to receive offerings and speak silently with the living.

The ka statue is a designed proxy: a body for a person who is no longer in the body, placed where the living can address it. The false door is the interface; the offering formula is the script. The relationship is one-sided by architecture, and the tomb is built to make it continuous. The dead cannot answer, but the living can return, and the return is the ritual.

The statue is not a portrait in the modern sense; it is a seat. The point is not likeness but availability. That distinction is the beginning of the long history of the stand-in that is treated as a presence.

c. 1350 BCE · Myth & Legend

Close ×

Akhenaten and the visible sun

Akhenaten elevated the sun disc Aten above the traditional gods and moved the centre of worship from the temple priesthood to the king and the visible disc.

Atenism is the first recorded attempt to replace a mediated pantheon with a single, visible object and a single royal interpreter. The traditional priests lost their role; the king became the one who knew what the disc wanted. The population was invited to see the sun and to address the king, not to negotiate with a crowd of deities. The relationship was one-sided in both directions: the disc could not answer, and the king spoke for it.

The Amarna period is also a warning about how quickly a mediated intimacy can be reversed. After Akhenaten's death, the old cults returned, his images were defaced, and the city was abandoned. The bond had been enforced from above rather than grown from below, which is why it did not survive its sponsor.

c. 800 BCE · Myth & Legend

Close ×

Homer and the voice in the room

The Homeric poems were performed, not read: a bard recited a familiar story to a room that already knew the characters and the outcome.

The audience did not meet Homer; it met a voice performing a world it already knew. The bard's presence, the formulaic epithets and the repetition made the heroes available as figures to admire, mourn and argue about. The bond is with the performance and with the persona of the singer as much as with Achilles. It is the earliest recorded structure in which a crowd gives its attention to one voice and receives a story in return.

The recitation is also a schedule. A poem that takes hours to perform holds a room together for that long, and the audience's memory carries the characters between performances. That continuity is the pre-print version of the serial: the figure exists because a community keeps returning to the same voice.

c. 534 BCE · Myth & Legend

Close ×

Thespis steps out of the chorus

Thespis is credited with stepping out of the chorus to become the first actor, turning a ritual ensemble into a single character an audience could watch.

Thespis is a name for a structural change: the chorus remains, but one performer steps forward and speaks as someone else. The audience now watches an individual rather than a collective ritual, and the individual is a fiction. The actor's body is present; the character is not. That gap is the first theatrical version of the mediated figure.

The story is reported by later writers, and the date is traditional. What survives is the form: a masked person speaking in the first person while the audience knows he is not the person. The audience's projection begins there.

c. 430 BCE · Myth & Legend

Close ×

Asclepius and the dream that visits

The cult of Asclepius offered healing through dream incubation: a patient slept in a temple and received a personal visitation from the god.

The Asklepieion turned illness into a private audience. The patient prepared, slept in the abaton, and reported a dream in which the god spoke or touched the body. The encounter was one-sided and intensely personal; the god appeared to the sleeper alone, and the cure was evidence that the visit had happened. The priest interpreted the dream but did not supply the presence.

The structure is durable because it gives the near side a role: the patient must sleep, remember and narrate. The far end is a figure who can be addressed but not questioned. Dream incubation is the ancient template for the therapeutic relationship in which the sufferer feels personally known by a being that exists only in the encounter.

c. 250 BCE–550 CE · Myth & Legend

Close ×

The wax masks in the hall

A Roman aristocrat had a wax mask of his own face taken while he was alive - usually in his thirties or forties, on taking office - and it was kept in a cupboard in the entrance hall beside a painted family tree and a label listing his offices. He never saw it worn. After his death, actors put it on and walked it in his funeral procession, in order of death, wearing the robes of the office he had held.

The best-documented one-sided attachment in this corpus, and thirteen thousand years later than the dog - which is the point. Everything here is checkable, because it was written down, and what it shows is how completely a bond can be built with someone who cannot answer. The mask never speaks: eye-holes and a gap between the lips were cut into it so that the actor could see and talk, and the inscription beside it did the conversing. Children grew up walking past it daily - Valerius Maximus has a man recalling that he called the dead his parents and drew his standing from their masks - and it had states: opened at festivals, hung with laurel on an election, closed during mourning. It was also an inheritance that changed address, going with a bride into her husband's house, and it was not uniformly flattering: Pliny's son was described as burdened by the masks he carried. No mask survives. All of it comes from authors.

c. 8 CE · Myth & Legend

Close ×

Narcissus and Echo: the image that cannot answer

Ovid's Metamorphoses tells of a nymph cursed to repeat only the last words spoken to her, and a youth who falls in love with his own reflection in a pool.

Echo has a voice but no sentence of her own: Juno's curse leaves her able to return the end of another person's speech, so every reply is borrowed. Narcissus is answered, but only by a surface that mirrors his own approach; when he reaches for it, it breaks. The myth separates two mechanisms the rest of this timeline keeps finding together: a far end that can only repeat, and a far end that can only reflect.

The attachment is intense because the near side supplies both halves of the exchange and misreads the result as consent. Ovid's sharper point is that Narcissus is not simply fooled. He loves an image he cannot touch, and the image is accurate. The tragedy is not a failure to tell reality from representation; it is an attachment that survives the distinction.

c. 100 CE · Myth & Legend

Close ×

The priest

A person who hears the specifics, performs the ritual, and knows the family history, on a repeating cycle.

The most complete parasocial arrangement available and it includes a uniform, a script and a confession. It is also the arrangement the most people are inside of, which is the strongest evidence that the form is universal rather than a symptom.

The structure is not the office but the repetition: the same person hears the same family's particulars year after year, and the relationship is real on one side and professional on the other. The priest is the first named role in which a stranger is licensed to know you intimately and is not required to be known back.

c. 160 CE · Myth & Legend

Close ×

Lucian and the puppet god

Lucian's Alexander the False Prophet describes a cult leader who staged a puppet god, Glycon, with a hidden speaking tube to give paying followers personal prophecies.

The puppet is an early machine for manufactured intimacy: a face, a voice, a private answer. The follower asks a question and receives a reply that seems to come from the god, while the operator supplies the voice. The fraud is not the point of the entry; the structure is. The far end is a staged body, and the near side pays for the feeling of being singled out.

Lucian's satire is also a reminder that the critique of mediated intimacy is ancient. The exposed mechanism does not make the desire disappear; it only moves the question to who is speaking.

787 CE · Myth & Legend

Close ×

The icon answers nothing

In 787 the Second Council of Nicaea ended the first phase of the Byzantine iconoclastic dispute and defined what an icon was for: the honour paid to the image passes to the figure it shows. Icons were lawful because in Christ the invisible God had been seen. The panel itself never answered anyone.

The council drew a line only the second phase of iconoclasm would redraw. The Byzantine dispute over images ran from the reign of the emperor Leo III in the 730s; the Second Council of Nicaea, summoned in 787, closed the first phase by declaring the veneration of icons lawful and orthodox. Its formula rests on a distinction the church still repeats: relative veneration (proskynesis - the honour, the greeting) was owed to the image, while true worship (latreia) belonged to God alone. The classical backing was Basil of Caesarea's sentence that the honour paid to the image passes to the prototype - the figure the image shows.

What the icon is for makes this site's subject in paint. The devotee stands before a panel understood, in the argument of John of Damascus and later the Studite writers, to participate in the figure it shows, so that a prayer said 'through' the image is addressed to somebody who is not in the room. The venerated panel cannot answer, and nobody expects it to; the whole doctrine runs on the reply being withheld here and heard elsewhere. The icon is a face in a church that speaks to nobody back - the painted absence this corpus already records in the empty-wall entry, arriving as an official theology rather than a habit.

The counter-argument is the one the council had to defeat, and it is kept on the entry rather than resolved. The iconoclasts charged the practice as idolatry; the council's answer was that honour directed through an image is not the worship of wood and pigment, and the plain reading of the ban on graven images was set against the Incarnation - the unseeable God had been seen in Christ. The settlement did not hold: the icons were banned again in 815 and restored for good only in 843. One political parallel the same argument used is worth keeping - the imperial portrait honoured an absent emperor exactly as an icon honours an absent Christ, which is the civic version of the same structure.

c. 1320 · Literature & Print

Close ×

Dante's Beatrice: the woman who becomes a guide

Dante's Divine Comedy turns a woman he met perhaps twice into a guide through Paradise.

Beatrice is the most extreme literary case of a real person converted into a figure: Dante barely knew her, and the poem gives her the authority of a guide, a judge and a destination. The reader is invited to love her as Dante does, which makes the attachment transitive. The beloved is at once a woman, a symbol and a voice in the text; the relationship is sustained by the poem rather than by any exchange.

The structure is the one the rest of this list keeps finding: the far end is silent, and the near end supplies the voice. What makes Dante's version distinctive is that the silence is not a failure. It is the condition of the poem's vision, and the reader is asked to accept the substitution as the price of admission.

c. 1327–1374 · Literature & Print

Close ×

Petrarch's Laura and the poetry of absence

Petrarch wrote hundreds of poems to Laura, a woman he may have seen once, and made the unreachable beloved the centre of a literary career.

Petrarch's Laura is a name and a face that the poems repeatedly approach and never possess. The sequence is built on absence: the speaker addresses a woman who cannot reply, and the reader is placed in the same posture. The sonnet form becomes a technology for keeping the attachment alive after the occasion has gone. It is the template for centuries of love poetry in which the beloved is a figure the reader is invited to desire.

The poems do not pretend the relationship is mutual. They make the non-answer the subject, and the reader's pleasure is in the precision of the longing. That is a different mechanism from the novel's immersive identification: here the distance is not a problem to be solved but the instrument that produces the feeling.

c. 1373–1438 · Literature & Print

Close ×

Margery Kempe

English woman who experienced what she described as an unbreakable bond with Jesus, was mocked for weeping in church, was reviled by her family, and in 1438 dictated a book about it that persuaded other women to do the same.

The single strongest real case in the catalogue, and it is eight hundred years early. A bond with a figure who never appears in the physical world. A text as the medium. Grief when the access was withdrawn, which is the Replika update. And a recruitment function: the book exists to make other women feel what she felt, which is what a parasocial relationship is for.

c. 1387-1400 · Literature & Print

Close ×

Chaucer's 'I': a narrator who is not the author

The Canterbury Tales frame a company of pilgrims with a first-person narrator, 'Chaucer', who reports their words and his own embarrassment.

The General Prologue creates a voice that is warm, gossipy and slightly foolish, and it addresses the reader as a companion on the road. The historical Chaucer is not that voice. The poem's 'I' is a persona who misremembers, apologises and invites the reader to judge the pilgrims alongside him. That gap is the first durable English example of mediated intimacy: the reader is spoken to by a constructed person who seems to have no screen between himself and the page.

The contract is conversational rather than dramatic. The narrator says he will tell the tale as he heard it and asks indulgence for plain speech, which positions the reader as a listener who has been let in. The frame does not require belief in the narrator, only the pleasant illusion that someone is talking to you rather than at you.

1418 · Literature & Print

Close ×

The Imitation of Christ and the inward companion

The Imitation of Christ teaches the reader to conduct a continuous inward conversation with Christ, in a voice that is intimate, demanding and entirely one-sided.

The book is a manual for internal dialogue. Its chapters alternate between the soul and Christ, and the reader is invited to take both parts. The voice is direct, personal and indifferent to public ceremony; the intimacy is achieved by turning the reader's attention inward. The companion is available at any hour because the companion is a text.

The Imitation is one of the most widely read Christian books after the Bible, and its method is the method of the parasocial bond: repeated address, a stable voice, and a relationship that is maintained by the reader's practice rather than by any reply. It is the devotional version of the serial: the same voice returns, and the reader keeps the appointment.

16th century (c. 1500–1600) · Literature & Print

Close ×

The ikiryō and the spirit that leaves

Japanese literature formalised the ikiryō, a living person's spirit that leaves the body to haunt or attach itself to a distant target, in Heian tales and later Noh.

The ikiryō is projection made narrative: jealousy or longing is so intense that it acquires a separate body and acts on the person who cannot be reached. In The Tale of Genji, Lady Rokujō's spirit attacks her rival; in Noh, the possessive spirit is staged as a mask and a voice. The target experiences the attachment as an invasion, while the source may not know what her spirit has done.

The motif is a pre-modern account of the boundary problem this site keeps finding: the near side's feeling becomes an action on the far side, but the action is not a relationship. The spirit can reach the target; it cannot receive an answer. The 16th-century Noh stage formalised a much older literary intuition.

1531 · Myth & Legend

Close ×

Am I not here, I who am your mother?

Four apparitions to a Chichimec farmer and one to his uncle, a single Nahuatl sentence that gave the devotion its title, and a cloth image the Catholic world has organised itself around ever since.

The entire relationship is address, and the founding story is one reply. According to the Nican Mopohua, written in Nahuatl, the Virgin appeared four times to Juan Diego, a Chichimec peasant, and once to his uncle Juan Bernardino, beginning on the morning of 9 December 1531. She spoke to him in his own language - Nahuatl, the language of the former Aztec empire - and identified herself as the mother of the very true deity. The sign he was sent to gather was Castile roses, not native to Mexico, blooming out of season on the summit of Tepeyac Hill; he carried them in his tilma, the cloak that bears the image venerated ever since. And the sentence the devotion is built on is her answer to his worry: '¿No estoy yo aquí que soy tu madre?' - 'Am I not here, I who am your mother?' - which the record calls the most famous phrase of the apparitions, and which is inscribed above the main entrance to the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe, on Tepeyac Hill in Mexico City, the most-visited Catholic shrine in the world and, the article says, the third most-visited sacred site. The shelf's test is address rather than watching, with the other end understood to hear, and that is the whole cult - built on one reply that nobody but a single man is recorded to have received. The evidence has been contested from the beginning. The 1556 inquiry records an attack on devotion to an image 'painted yesterday by the Indian Marcos'; Sahagún recorded his suspicion that it was 'a Satanic invention to cloak idolatry under the confusion of this name, Tonantzin' - 'They come from distant lands to this Tonantzin as in olden times'. Juan Diego himself is doubted: Zumárraga's own writings never mention him, the 1556 inquiry omits him, he appears in no document before the mid-17th century, and in 1996 the abbot of the Basilica was forced to resign after saying Juan Diego was 'a symbol, not a reality'. None of it stopped anything. In 1754 the Sacred Congregation of Rites confirmed the apparitions and the December 12 feast; Leo XIII granted the decree of canonical coronation in 1887, executed in 1895; and in 2002 Juan Diego was canonised as the first indigenous American saint. The image's own history is a record of being handled, defended and examined. In 1887-88 the ten-point crown painted on the Virgin's head disappeared - the change was noticed on 23 February 1888, and eventually a painter confessed on his deathbed that a clergyman had instructed him to remove it. In 1921 a bomb left under the tilma by an anti-Catholic secularist damaged the altar and left the image unharmed; the survival is called miraculous by devotees. In 1981, examining the cloth under infrared light, Philip Serna Callahan and Jody Brant Smith found no trace of sizing or sketching underneath the paint, and no explanation for the original parts of the image or their preservation. That is the honest shape of the whole entry: the most-visited shrine in the Catholic world rests on a Nahuatl text and a piece of cloth, and the address has been going up to both, undiminished, for five hundred years.

1582 · Myth & Legend

Close ×

John Dee, Edward Kelley and the angel conversations

John Dee and Edward Kelley used a crystal globe and an obsidian mirror to hold conversations with angels, recording thousands of words of a claimed celestial language.

The scrying sessions are a technology of mediated presence: a surface, a seer, a scribe and a voice that is always elsewhere. Kelley saw the figures; Dee wrote what they said. The relationship was one-sided, repeated and bureaucratic, with dates, alphabets and instructions. The angel was available on schedule.

Enochian is the Renaissance version of the channel: the medium supplies the access, the scholar supplies the record, and the far end never appears in the room. The fact that the conversations are so detailed is what makes them convincing and what makes them a record of the near side's mind.

1605 · Literature & Print

Close ×

Don Quixote reads himself into a knight

Cervantes's Alonso Quixano reads so many chivalric romances that he resolves to become a knight-errant, and the world has to negotiate with the fiction he is living in.

Quixote is not merely a fan of romances. He uses them as a script for conduct, renaming himself, arming himself and interpreting inns as castles. The comedy is that other people can see the gap and he cannot. The parasocial structure runs in the opposite direction from most of this timeline: instead of attaching to a distant figure, he attaches to a genre and then demands that the genre's rules be honoured by everyone he meets.

Cervantes makes the reader complicit. We are given the fiction and the correction in the same sentence, so we occupy the position of the sane household and the position of the man who prefers the story. That double occupancy is the earliest sustained literary account of what it feels like to know a representation is not real and to keep acting as if it were.

1740 · Literature & Print

Close ×

Virtue rewarded

The novel that turned its readers into a correspondent. Pamela Andrews writes home about her master's pursuit, and the reader takes the seat of the parents - receiving every letter, sending none. Published anonymously in November 1740, it became the first English best-seller and the first novel whose readers wrote back demanding more of it.

The form is a correspondence the reader reads from the far end of. Richardson was a printer who took a commission in 1739 to compile a volume of model "familiar letters" for people too unskilled to write their own, and the germ of Pamela was a short run of letters from a servant daughter asking her father's advice about her master's advances. He kept the epistolary shape and changed its address: the letters are written not to a lover but to Pamela's parents, who are offstage, at a distance, and never answer inside the book. The reader is put in that seat - handed a life in letters addressed to somebody else, with no way to write back - which is this site's subject arriving in the first novel most of its readers ever meet.

The reception is a record of attachment, and it is unusually well documented. The book is, on the Cambridge edition's own description, "perhaps the most influential novel published in Britain in the eighteenth century" and "on its first publication in 1740 ... an immediate bestseller"; it ran to five editions in its first year and produced what the University of Michigan project calls a "'Pamela' rage," with Pamela motifs on teacups and fans. The world was said to divide into "Pamelists and Antipamelists." A village blacksmith, the oft-repeated anecdote runs, read it aloud on his anvil through the summer evenings to an attentive crowd and set the parish bells ringing at the happy ending. And the readers did not stay passive: the unauthorized continuations and parodies - Fielding's Shamela, Haywood's Anti-Pamela, Kelly's Pamela's Conduct in High Life - drew a sequel from Richardson himself, Pamela in her Exalted Condition, in 1742. The audience's want bent the text.

The counter-argument is that Pamela belongs to the history of the novel, not to this site: its importance is form, consent and class, and the people who wrote back wrote to Richardson, not to a girl who never existed. It is a fair objection and the entry's claim is narrower than it looks. What it files is a structure - a one-sided correspondence the reader reads from the parents' end - and a documented public that formed an attachment and then wrote to keep it going. The letters in the book are addressed to figures who cannot reply; the letters out of the book were addressed to a man who could, and did, and wrote two more volumes because of them. Both are this site's shape. Contestable, and recorded as such.

1748 · Literature & Print

Close ×

Clarissa dies and the readers write back

Samuel Richardson's Clarissa is an epistolary novel whose heroine dies, and readers wrote to Richardson begging him to spare her.

Clarissa is the first mass reading experience in which the audience feels entitled to intervene in a fictional life. The novel is a bundle of letters, so the reader is already inside a correspondence; when Clarissa dies, the letters stop and the reader is left with the grief of a survivor. Richardson's readers wrote as if he could revise the ending.

The letters to Richardson are the evidence that the bond was treated as a relationship with an obligation. The author is the one who can keep the character alive, and the reader's appeal is addressed to him as a person. The novel's form made the request feel natural.

1774 · Literature & Print

Close ×

Werther and the costume of grief

Goethe's epistolary novel made a young man's unrequited love and suicide a European sensation, and readers copied both the feeling and the clothes.

Werther writes letters to a friend and to Lotte, and the reader is placed inside an intimacy that has only one correspondent. The novel's form is the mechanism: no omniscient narrator corrects him, so the reader lives at his level of certainty. When the book became a fashion, the clothing style described in it turned a private attachment into a public costume, and the reported copycat deaths gave the reception its later name, the Werther effect.

The important point is not that readers were foolish. It is that print can distribute a whole emotional grammar - what to feel, what to wear, how to die - and that the grammar arrives with the intimacy of a letter. The copycat reports are themselves disputed; Goethe's biographer Rüdiger Safranski called the Werther effect a persistent rumour, which is the right caution for a story the culture wanted to be true.

1812–1824 · Literature & Print

Byron and the poet as his own hero

Lord Byron woke up famous after Childe Harold's Pilgrimage and became the first poet whose readers treated the author as the hero of his own work.

Byron's readers did not separate the poet from the brooding, exiled narrator of his poems. The Byronic hero gave them a template for feeling, and Byron's own life supplied the sequel. The attachment was to a persona that the poems and the press built together. When he died at Missolonghi, the mourning was for a figure who had been available chiefly through print.

The mechanism is identification with a posture rather than with a plot. Readers did not need to meet Byron to know how he suffered; the poems told them, and the newspapers confirmed it. The poet became a character whose continuing story was published in instalments called biography.

1830s-1850s · Literature & Print

Close ×

Dickens, the serial, and the death of Little Nell

Dickens published his novels in monthly and weekly parts, making the next instalment a shared appointment; the death of Little Nell in The Old Curiosity Shop became a public bereavement.

Serial publication turned reading into a schedule. A huge audience met the same characters in the same week, and the gap between parts was a real interval in which the characters continued to exist without the reader. That interval is the engine: it produces anticipation, conjecture and a sense of ongoing relationship rather than a single transaction.

The death of Nell made the mechanism visible. Readers mourned a child who had never existed, and the story that American crowds met the incoming ship asking whether she had died is repeated so often that it has become part of the reception even where the evidence is thin. Dickens's later public readings, where audiences were reported to faint at the murder of Nancy, moved the same attachment into a room with a live body in it.

Phase
2 · Literature, Early Mass Print & Stage Magic
Date note
1812 is Dickens's birth year; the serial phenomenon begins with Pickwick in 1836.

1840–1847 · Music & Fan Culture

Close ×

Lisztomania and the souvenir body

Franz Liszt's concert tours produced scenes of fainting, souvenir-collecting and crowd frenzy that the press named Lisztomania.

Liszt played in public and then let the public take pieces of him: gloves, handkerchiefs, locks of hair, broken piano strings. The performance was not only the music but the availability of the performer's body. Heinrich Heine coined the term, and the pattern it describes - a crowd treating an artist as a personal possession - is the direct ancestor of the pop idol.

The souvenir is the mechanism made physical. A glove or a string is not the person, but it is a piece of the person's presence that can be carried away. The audience's attachment is to a body it has seen at a distance, and the object is the substitute for a reply.

Phase
2 · Literature, Early Mass Print & Stage Magic

Jane Eyre speaks to one reader at a time

Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre addressed the reader directly in its opening pages and made a fictional woman's interior life a mass reading experience.

The novel begins with 'There was no possibility of taking a walk that day', and the reader is placed inside Jane's head before any plot arrives. The intimacy is grammatical: first person, present-tense feeling, a narrator who confides. Readers wrote to Brontë as if to Jane, and the book's success was partly the success of a voice that seemed to be speaking to one person at a time.

The address is not a trick. It is the form's basic offer: a stranger's interior life, available for the length of the book. What changed with the novel was the scale - thousands of readers could receive the same confidential voice and each feel personally addressed.

1848 · Myth & Legend

Close ×

The Fox sisters and the paid séance

In 1848 the Fox sisters in Hydesville, New York, claimed to communicate with a spirit through rapping sounds, and the séance became a paid public ritual.

Spiritualism turned the absence of the dead into a channel. The medium supplied the voice, the knock or the table tilt; the sitter supplied the name and the grief. The encounter was intimate and evidential at once: a specific deceased person was said to be present, and the payment made the access repeatable. The far end could not be checked, which is what made the ritual portable.

The Fox sisters later confessed and recanted, and the movement survived them. The important structure is not the truth of the raps but the arrangement: a paid mediator, a private message, and a client who leaves with the feeling of having been addressed. That is the template for the modern medium and for a great deal of platform intimacy.

1850s–1860s · Literature & Print

Close ×

The carte de visite and the face in the album

Cheap photographic portraits on card mounts let ordinary people collect the faces of the famous and keep them in albums at home.

The carte de visite was the first mass-produced photographic portrait, and the album was its living room. A family could own a likeness of a monarch, an actor or a general and look at it repeatedly. The photograph did not move or speak, but it made the famous face a domestic object. It is the ancestor of the poster, the trading card and the profile picture.

The album is the important part. Collecting turns a set of strangers into a personal collection, and the collector supplies the order and the attention. The face is available for return visits, which is the minimum condition of a parasocial relationship.

1852 · Literature & Print

Close ×

Uncle Tom's Cabin and the mass feeling for strangers

Harriet Beecher Stowe's novel sold in enormous numbers and turned its characters into figures of public grief and political argument.

Uncle Tom's Cabin was read aloud in parlours and adapted for the stage, so the same characters arrived in different rooms at the same time. Readers wept for Little Eva and argued about Tom as if they knew them. The novel's political force came through attachment: a mass audience was asked to feel for people it had never met, and the feeling was organised by a book.

The stage adaptations widened the audience and fixed the characters' images. A reader who had never opened the novel could still know Little Eva from a play or a print. The figure became public property, which is the condition of a mass-mediated bond.

1858–1870 · Literature & Print

Close ×

Dickens reads himself into the room

Dickens toured Britain and America reading his own work aloud, and audiences were reported to faint, weep and treat the readings as visits from the characters.

The reading tour converted a private act of reading into a room with a famous body in it. Dickens performed the murder of Nancy and the death of Paul Dombey; the audience's reaction was part of the event. The bond was not with a character alone but with the author as the person who could make the characters present. The tour is the bridge between serial reading and modern celebrity appearance.

The reports of fainting are the useful detail because they show the body answering a fiction as if it were a presence. The reader had already spent months with the characters; the reading gave that attachment a face and a voice in the same room. It is the moment the author becomes the medium.

Miss Havisham

A woman in Great Expectations who is left jilted at the altar, stops eating, ages, and arranges to be found the way she was on her wedding day - decades later, in a wedding dress, in a darkened room.

The most complete fictional treatment of the object of a parasocial bond being a person who was never real, and of the grief outliving the reasons for it. She is not a metaphor for a fictional character, she is a person who has mistaken her own wedding for a plot.

The shrine is the mechanism: a woman stops the clocks and keeps the room as it was, which is what an unrequited attachment does when it has a house to do it in.

Pepper's Ghost and the body that is only light

Pepper's Ghost used angled glass and lighting to project a translucent figure onto a stage, making a ghost appear to share the room with the actors.

Pepper's Ghost is the ancestor of the hologram and the augmented stage: the technical production of a person who is present to the eye and absent to every other sense. The audience knows the trick and still feels the arrival.

1891 · Music & Fan Culture

Close ×

The Divine Sarah

Sarah Bernhardt toured more like a head of state than a player: when she sailed for New York in 1891 the crossing was covered the way a royal visit is, and 'Divine Sarah' was by then the whole public's phrase for her. Mark Twain's note put it exactly - there were five kinds of actresses, and Sarah Bernhardt. An idol built at distance.

The most famous face the pre-cinema stage could make. Born in Paris in 1844, Bernhardt was by the 1870s the figure the international press called Divine Sarah - Oscar Wilde's 1879 poem of that name had her crowned with lilies at the feet of audiences who would never see her act in a room, and a French paper called her a national institution. Her motto was 'Quand Même' - 'in spite of everything' - which the torments of a career turned into a legend of refusal.

The 1891 tour was the idol arriving. In 1891 she left Le Havre on 15 October aboard the L'Amérique on her way to America, and the arrival was covered in the register of a state visit: one account of these tours records the homage shown her as the kind 'usually reserved for royalty', applause and press for a woman most of the auditorium had only met through prints, reviews and playbills. Distance is the mechanism - the audience knew the surface better than the woman, and a finished public surface is exactly what a parasocial idol is made of.

She stood at the seam between the printed and the cinematic star. Mark Twain's tribute, written for a tour programme, ranked her apart from every other class of actress, and the cinema that arrived within a generation inherited the structure: the same manufactured distance, the same schedule of manufactured encounters, the same audience that never arrived in time for the making. The counter-argument - that she was simply the greatest actress of her age and the devotion was earned on stage - is kept on the entry. The claim here is narrower: her fame was distributed by the print machinery this corpus files everywhere else under the idol, which makes her the theatre's first systematic case of it.

1893 · Literature & Print

Close ×

Conan Doyle kills Sherlock Holmes

Conan Doyle killed Sherlock Holmes at Reichenbach Falls in 1893, and readers responded with a public campaign that forced the character's return.

The Final Problem is the first mass-media death that a fan audience treated as a personal loss and a breach of contract. Readers wore black armbands, wrote letters and cancelled subscriptions; Doyle was accosted in the street. The character had been serialised for six years, and the audience's relationship with him was a scheduled habit. Killing him was experienced as an abandonment.

Doyle resisted for eight years, then brought Holmes back in 1901 and 1903. The return is the proof of the mechanism: a fictional figure can be killed by an author and restored by an audience, because the audience's attachment is part of the character's life. The author owns the text; the readers own the habit.

The "Picture Postcard Craze" & Instant Visual Collecting

The universal adoption of cheap postcard postage triggered an international collecting phenomenon.

The universal adoption of cheap postcard postage triggered an international collecting phenomenon. It turned celebrity gazing into a tactile, pocketable, and daily postal habit.

1907 · Politics & News

Close ×

Florence Lawrence ("The Biograph Girl") & The Invention of the Movie Star

Early film studios intentionally kept actors' names secret to avoid paying higher wages. Audiences, however, recognized actress Florence Lawrence across multiple short films and wrote hundreds of letters to Biograph Studios asking for the identity.

Early film studios intentionally kept actors' names secret to avoid paying higher wages. Audiences, however, recognized actress Florence Lawrence across multiple short films and wrote hundreds of letters to Biograph Studios asking for the identity of "The Biograph Girl." When producer Carl Laemmle lured her to IMP Studios in 1910 and leaked a publicity stunt claiming she had died in a streetcar accident, he launched the modern movie star publicity apparatus.

1911 · Broadcast & Film

Close ×

Thousands came to gawk at the empty wall

An Italian workman walked out of the Louvre with the painting under his coat, and the wall it had hung on went on drawing a crowd: four iron hooks, no picture, and thousands of people come to look at the hooks anyway. The papers printed the absence, and when she came back she had become public property - the first mass art icon, made by a thief rather than by a painter.

A crowd stood in front of an empty wall, and that is the whole entry. The four hooks were still there and people came to look at them - "thousands of people came to gawk at the empty wall where the painting had once hung". L'Illustration printed the question the absence had raised for it: "What audacious criminal, what mystifier, what maniac collector, what insane lover, has committed this abduction?" A picture nobody could see was being discussed in the language reserved for a kidnapping, which is the correct language for the situation and is also the first time in this corpus that a crowd's attention is described as a taking rather than as a looking.

The scale is recorded twice and the two records do not agree. One has "more than 100,000 people viewed it" after the return; the other has "at least 120,000 people went to see the painting in the first two days after it was returned". Both are kept, because the disagreement is the evidence - numbers that size are what a public looks like once an object has become a story. The record also disagrees about the theft itself: one man, or three. That disagreement is kept too, and neither version changes a word of the entry, which is about the wall rather than about who carried her out of it.

What the theft produced is the sentence worth having. As the account the entry leans on puts it, "The Mona Lisa had left the Louvre a work of art. She returned as public property, the first mass art icon." Satirical postcards, a short film and cabaret songs followed, and "popular culture seized upon the theft and turned high art into mass art." The image went on doing the work the canvas used to do, and the canvas came back as something people queued to be near.

Peruggia is the one attachment in the record that answers itself. He said he had fallen "a victim to her smile" and feasted his eyes on his treasure every evening, which is a one-sided tie describing itself out loud and in a courtroom's vocabulary. The crowd had the same tie and no sentence for it, which is what the queue in front of the hooks was. She was not there for either of them, and being not-there is the whole of the arrangement.

1914 · Broadcast & Film

Close ×

A doodle of you used as your address

By 1917 nine out of ten men at a costume ball came as him, a hold-up man in Cincinnati borrowed his costume as a disguise, and in 1916 somebody was paging him in more than eight hundred hotels at the same moment. Later, fans sent letters with a doodle of his face where the address should have been. The likeness had stopped being a picture and started being an instruction.

The silhouette was usable. That is the entry. The Tramp first appears in Kid Auto Races at Venice, filmed on 11 January 1914 and released on 7 February; by 1917 the costume was common enough to be a costume of record - "most of the girls came as Annette Kellerman, the swimming star, and nine out of ten men came as Charlie Chaplin." In February 1917 the same costume was used as a disguise by a hold-up man in Cincinnati. A likeness that exists only on a screen cannot be worn by a robber. This one could, and that is the difference between being famous and being an instruction.

The same period that produced the robbers produced the diagnosis. About 12 November 1916 the Boston Society for Psychical Research was investigating "certain phenomena connected with the simultaneous paging of Mr Charles Chaplin, motion picture comedian, in more than 800 large hotels of the United States" - one man being asked for in eight hundred hotels at once, from the Atlantic to the Pacific and the Canadian boundary to the Gulf - and the Kansas City Star asked the next day whether readers had had "the Chaplin-itis?" Robinson's account of the period has theatres "promoting the Chaplin vogue by sponsoring amateur Charlie look-alike contests"; Chaplin himself said he was "tempted to give lessons in the Chaplin walk."

The contest story is told two ways and both are here. The Chaplin archive's own press clippings from 1918 record Mary Pickford telling a dinner in London that he had entered a Chaplin walk contest at a fair in the United States and came in twentieth; the version everybody repeats has him coming in third, which Snopes rates Unproven and traces to a magazine post from December 2022. The famous version is the one that needed no source, and the documented one is second-hand from a friend. Neither number changes what the contests were for: an audience competing to be the nearest copy of a man who was not there to judge it.

The mail is where the likeness becomes infrastructure. In a 1932 feature on "Hollywood's Funny Fan Mail", Clara Bow was receiving about 35,000 letters a month; Maurice Chevalier's arrived with no address whatever, just his picture on the envelope; Clark Gable's were addressed to "Valentino the Second". An address that works without a street is a likeness doing a job, and by the 1950s a doodle of Chaplin's face was being used as the address on letters sent to him at the Savoy Hotel. This entry does not claim what became of that post; the point is only that it was thought to be enough to send.

1914 · Broadcast & Film

Close ×

Known to more people than any other woman in history

The first film performer whose value could be counted instead of guessed. She was on the cover of the New York Dramatic Mirror in 1911, an honour then kept for theatrical stars; by 1916 her fan following had become ten thousand dollars a week, half her film profits and a production company of her own. The audience was never asked for any of it, and every line of the contract exists because of it.

The fan worship is in the contract. St. John's line, as the American Experience page quotes it, is the scale the entry works from: Pickford was "known to more people and loved by more people than any other woman that has been in all history." Reach was the asset, and reach was countable. In 1911 she was the first movie star to adorn the cover of the New York Dramatic Mirror, an honour "previously bestowed only on theatrical stars" - the trade press had already decided that a moving-picture player could carry a cover, and the sentence that records it is careful to say what the honour used to be worth.

Then 1914 and Tess of the Storm Country. The record says the picture "caused a sensation", that it "created fan worship that had never before been witnessed", and that the success "gave Mary Pickford incredible bargaining power"; by 1916 she had "a $10,000 a week salary, 50% of her film profits, and her own production company." The chronology is kept rather than resolved: her foundation dates the renegotiation to May 1916, another account dates a contract at 24 June 1916 with a guarantee of $1.04 million. Both are here, because a date and a number that disagree are the ordinary state of a contract nobody was meant to read. United Artists followed in February 1919, with Fairbanks, Chaplin, Griffith and Hart.

The other side of it is why this is not a portrait. When the company she co-founded had its way, it would "pressure Pickford to limit herself artistically, playing roles she knew her fans would love." Nobody voted and the studio obeyed anyway. That is the shape of the whole period: an audience made sovereign and unaware of it, consulted through a contract clause rather than through a question. By 1927 the highs were over, and what the constraint had been buying was visible from the outside.

1914 · Broadcast & Film

Close ×

Pearl White and the weekly peril

Pearl White starred in The Perils of Pauline and the serial form made weekly cinema audiences return to the same endangered heroine.

The serial ended each week with the heroine in danger, and the audience had to come back to find out whether she survived. That is a scheduled relationship: the character continues to exist between episodes, and the viewer carries her forward. Pearl White performed her own stunts and the press made her daredevil image part of the story, so the actress and the character became one figure.

The cliffhanger is a contract. It asks the audience to care across a gap, and the caring is what turns a film into a habit. The serial heroine is one of the first screen figures whose survival is a weekly public question.

1921 · Broadcast & Film

Close ×

Cordially yours, Betty Crocker

In 1921 a flour company's advertising department needed one woman's name for the kitchen advice its all-female home-service staff was already writing. Betty Crocker was a signature and a persona, not a person: she answered letters, then took a radio voice in 1924, and gave millions a correspondent who signed herself "Cordially yours."

The reply existed before the name did. In late October 1921 Gold Medal Flour ran a jigsaw-puzzle advertisement in The Saturday Evening Post; Washburn-Crosby received 30,000 completed puzzles and, with them, several hundred letters of cooking questions. The advertising department asked the board to create a personality that the women answering the letters could all sign, as the company's own account puts it. "Crocker" honoured a retired company director, William G. Crocker; "Betty" was chosen because it sounded friendly; employees competed to submit the signature and Florence Lindberg's was adopted, and is still in use. The replies, written by a home-service department of home economists, went out signed "Cordially Yours, Betty Crocker" - a real hand typing under a name no woman owned.

Then the persona was given a voice, which is what makes it a bond rather than a byline. In 1924 the company helped a local radio station out of bankruptcy, renamed it WCCO, and put Betty Crocker on daytime radio's first cooking show, "the Betty Crocker Cooking School of the Air"; Blanche Ingersoll was its first voice, the program spread to thirteen regional stations, and from 1927 it ran on the fledgling NBC network for twenty-four years, with more than a million listeners enrolled. Each station had its own Betty Crocker reading the same scripts from Minneapolis, and letters - now from across the Midwest - kept arriving. General Mills' own description of the effect is this entry's best line: her voice on the air "was like the woman next door dropping in for a morning visit to share a new recipe."

This is the brand-as-character mechanism at its founding, decades before the corpus had a name for it. A corporation was given a face and a tone so that a customer relationship would have a subject, and the entry files it as an instance of that later mechanism with the practice dated to the year the signature was drawn. The tie is one-sided in the way that matters: the reader attached to a woman who did not exist, and the reply, however real the labour behind it, came from the persona rather than the person. The counter - that a home economist really did answer, so the bond was two-way - loses because the far end of the reader's attachment was Betty, and Betty could not answer as herself; the correspondence ran under a single invented name for exactly that purpose. Contestable, and recorded as such.

1922 · Broadcast & Film

Close ×

Most faithfully, Rin Tin Tin

A German Shepherd found on a battlefield became one of the biggest silent-film stars, and the fan mail that arrived for him was answered with a glossy portrait signed by a paw.

The credit read 'Played by himself', and the fan mail was answered by a paw. Rin Tin Tin was found in a French field in September 1918 by Lee Duncan, an American soldier, and came home with him; the dog got his first film work in 1922, when a director needed something more reliable than a camera-shy wolf in The Man from Hell's River, and his first starring role - Where the North Begins, opposite Claire Adams in 1923 - made him a star. A dog who could not read received the mail of a matinee idol, by the thousands of letters a week, and the reply was manufactured exactly the way a human star's would have been: a glossy portrait, signed with an inked paw print, over the line Duncan wrote for him - 'Most faithfully, Rin Tin Tin'. The studio leaned on him whenever it got into trouble, and the films were known inside the trade as the mortgage lifters; by 1927 the most sophisticated film audience in Europe had made him the most popular actor in Berlin. The audience knew perfectly well he was a dog, and that was the condition of the whole thing. The one performer in this corpus who ever came physically close to answering back was the one who could not possibly understand what he was being addressed for, and the attachment has outlived him by a century of dog after dog. Two honesty notes belong here. The sources disagree on the count of his films - the New Yorker gives twenty-three silent pictures, Wikipedia twenty-seven Hollywood films - and the battlefield rescue is Duncan's own story, retold with variations ever since.

1924 · Broadcast & Film

Close ×

The radio church of Sister Aimee

Her church went on the air on 6 February 1924: KFSG - 'Kall Foursquare Gospel' - broadcasting at 500 watts from Angelus Temple, listener-supported one day at a time. She is credited by her own church as the first woman to preach a sermon on radio (1922), and after the first broadcast the letters came from other states and other countries, cataloguing where the signal had been heard.

A church built to be heard at a distance. Aimee Semple McPherson had preached on Los Angeles radio before owning a station, and her church's history credits her as the first woman to preach a sermon over the radio, on the Rockridge station in Oakland in April 1922. In February 1924 KFSG went on the air from Angelus Temple - a 500-watt Western Electric transmitter whose dedication named its reach, 'the people of the United States, Canada, Alaska, Mexico, Panama, Hawaii, South Sea Islands'. The congregation had raised the roughly $25,000 to build it.

The letters were the reply channel, and they were the audience. In the early 1920s a station learned who was listening from the mail: cards, telegrams and letters reporting where the signal was received. The record kept for KFSG includes letters from Illinois, Indiana, Pennsylvania and New Zealand describing when the broadcast was heard and what it meant - 'We do hope to hear you soon again', one wrote, and a listener in Indiana asked who the woman preacher had been. The station answered its mail through volunteer church members, and it was sponsored day by day by listeners through the Radio Missionary Society, with patrons booked months ahead.

The mechanism is a congregational 'you' at a distance. The church addressed the radio congregation as assembled even though the far end could not answer: in Angelus Temple the pastor asked 'Do you pledge to live clean Christian lives for God?' and the answer - 'We do' - came back from a room the radio listeners could not join. That is the presenter mechanism with a congregation in it: second-person grammar aimed at an unseen audience, engineered on a schedule. The competing placement, the idol, fails because the sermons were live and ongoing - an address from somebody who believed herself perceived, not a finished body of work. One honesty note is kept: the famous 'minions of Satan' telegram to Secretary Hoover over a wavelength dispute is recorded by radio historians as legend rather than fact, and KFSG was never actually taken off the air.

1926 · Broadcast & Film

Close ×

Valentino's funeral and the invention of screen grief

When Rudolph Valentino died in 1926 at thirty-one, crowds besieged the funeral home in New York and the mourning became a public event.

Valentino was known through a projected image larger than life and a press apparatus that sold him as 'the Great Lover'. The grief was for a man most mourners had never heard speak in person, and it was organised by the same industry that had made him. The funeral turned a private attachment into a public ritual with a script: flowers, fainting, a viewing, a queue.

The detail that makes it a parasocial case rather than a celebrity obituary is Pola Negri's performance of bereavement. She claimed an engagement Valentino had not publicly confirmed, and the claim was accepted because the audience already had a relationship with him that needed a story. The screen image outlived the body and immediately began to be managed.

1927 · Music & Fan Culture

Close ×

The baseball the papers built

In 1927 Babe Ruth hit sixty home runs and became the most replayed figure in a game most fans knew through print. His bylined column ran in syndication, much of it ghostwritten, and radio was beginning to carry him into rooms the stadium never reached. The 1920s press manufactured a 'hot romance' and he was its star.

The season the man and the persona arrived together. Ruth's 1927 season - sixty home runs in a 154-game schedule, a single-season record that stood until Roger Maris hit sixty-one in 1961, with the Yankees' Murderers' Row around him - is the on-field anchor this entry leans on without being about. The subject is the parallel figure the press built, because most of the people who loved him never saw him play.

The printed voice was another man's. Through the 1920s Ruth's byline ran across the country in syndicated columns and serials, and much of that copy was ghostwritten - the 'Babe Ruth' column was substantially the work of Christy Walsh, his agent, who organised the ghosted pieces under Ruth's name. A reader opening the sports page met a voice signed 'Babe Ruth' that Babe Ruth had not written, which is the manufactured reply end of a one-sided tie arriving in sports journalism: the attention felt answered, and the answer was an agency.

Radio and the syndicated page made the tie work at distance. Baseball went on the air in the 1920s, and Ruth's name travelled ahead of him by broadcast and by print - this entry records the 1920 film 'Headin' Home' as the star's celluloid echo of the same reach. The deeper claim, read from the thesis this entry draws on, is that the newspapers of the 1920s manufactured what one account calls a 'hot romance between sport and the public'. The counter-argument - that Ruth's fame was earned by a bat, not by columns - is real and kept on the entry; the point is narrower, that the relationship hundreds of thousands had with him ran through contributed copy and broadcast names rather than through a seat in a ballpark.

1929–1946 · Broadcast & Film

Close ×

The Goldbergs and the neighbours who wrote back

The Goldbergs brought a Jewish family into American living rooms as a daily radio serial, and listeners treated them as neighbours.

The show's intimacy was domestic: a family, a kitchen, a daily problem, a familiar voice. Listeners sent baby gifts, condolence letters and recipe advice to the characters' home address, which is the clearest evidence that the fiction had become a social relationship. The household was fictional; the address was real enough to receive mail.

The Goldbergs is the bridge between the soap opera and the sitcom: a serial family whose ordinary life is the plot. The audience's attachment is to the routine, not to a single star.

1930 · Broadcast & Film

The soap opera

A form built almost entirely by women, for women, and treated as unserious for fifty years. Daily episodes, fixed slots, cliffhangers, characters written in indefinitely and never resolved.

The origin of the entire research tradition, and it started as a footnote about daytime television that nobody thought was important. The rhythm is the mechanism: a fixed slot and an unresolved story, repeated daily, is a relationship with a schedule. It is also the reason the phrase 'soap opera' is now an insult rather than a description.

The daily schedule is the mechanism: a fixed slot, an unresolved story and a character who continues without you. The sponsor's name in the title made the relationship commercial at the level of the form, not merely at the ad break.

1933–1939 · Broadcast & Film

Calling All Cars and the audience in the chase

Calling All Cars was an early radio crime series that invited listeners into a weekly manhunt, with a host who addressed the audience directly.

The show's innovation was the call to the audience: listeners were invited to participate in the chase, and the radio voice made the police procedure feel like a conversation. The boundary between the story and the listener's room was thin. The program is an early example of broadcast content that asks the audience to act.

The seed list dates this to 1983; the series ran from 1933 to 1939. The correction matters because the call-in form is a radio invention, not a 1980s television one.

1933 · Politics & News

Close ×

The Fireside Chats: the president in the living room

Franklin Roosevelt used radio to address the nation in an informal, conversational register, beginning on 12 March 1933 during the banking crisis.

The chats worked because they did not sound like a broadcast. Roosevelt spoke slowly, used plain language and addressed listeners as 'my friends'; radio dissolved the distance between the White House and the parlour while leaving the speaker entirely unable to hear the reply. The intimacy was real in its effects and one-way in its structure.

This is the state's version of the mechanism: a leader who appears to explain himself personally to you, in your own home, at a moment of fear. The audience's sense of being addressed is not a mistake - the address is genuine - but the relationship is not reciprocal, and the warmth is also an instrument of governance.

1936 · Politics & News

Edward VIII abdicates into the microphone

Edward VIII addressed the nation by radio to explain why he was giving up the throne for Wallis Simpson.

The abdication speech is a monarch speaking personally, in his own voice, about a private choice. The audience sat in silence around the radio, and the form made the constitutional crisis feel like a confession. The king was not asking for a reply; he was asking to be understood.

The speech is a landmark in political intimacy: the state's most formal figure using the most domestic medium to explain himself. The intimacy is real, and it is also a performance of legitimacy at the moment legitimacy is being surrendered.

1938 · Broadcast & Film

Close ×

The War of the Worlds and the audience that believed the voice

Orson Welles's Mercury Theatre broadcast on 30 October 1938 presented H. G. Wells's invasion as a series of news bulletins, and some listeners took it as reportage.

The broadcast exploited the authority of the radio news voice: it interrupted dance music, used place names and interviewed supposed experts. The panic was real but much smaller than the legend; the audience research estimated that a minority of listeners were frightened and an even smaller number fled. The case matters because the mechanism is auditory trust, not credulity in general: a familiar voice in a familiar format can override what the listener knows.

The legend has since become a story about mass hysteria, which is itself a parasocial artefact - a public that enjoys believing it is uniquely suggestible. The documented broadcast is more interesting: most listeners changed the station, and the ones who stayed were often reassured by the very conventions that frightened others.

A character who cannot die, printed in a newspaper, read by a generation of children on the same day.

1939–1945 · Politics & News

Close ×

Lord Haw-Haw and the traitor in the room

William Joyce broadcast Nazi propaganda to Britain from Berlin, and his upper-class English voice made him a strangely familiar nightly presence.

Lord Haw-Haw's power was the voice, not the argument. Listeners tuned in to hear a traitor speak in their own accent, and the familiarity was the discomfort: he sounded like a BBC announcer, a teacher, a neighbour. The broadcasts were addressed to a nation and received by individuals in private, which is the structure of the intimate radio talk.

The wartime audience often listened to mock him, which is still a relationship. The mockery is a way of managing the fact that the voice is inside the room. Joyce was hanged in 1946; the broadcasts are a reminder that the intimate register can be weaponised without the audience ever being fooled.

1940 · Politics & News

Close ×

This is London

The live rooftop broadcasts that carried the Blitz into American homes, and the sign-off that made a reporter and a city the same thing.

Every broadcast went out live, because the sound of the raid was the report. Murrow was, in Philip Seib's account, the only journalist allowed to broadcast live during the air raids on London - a permission arranged with Winston Churchill's intervention - and the recording technology of the day was, in Neal Conan's word and with Seib's agreement, klutzy; Murrow's argument was the silence and the anti-aircraft fire, transmitted while they were happening. The opening line, 'This is London', with its deliberate pause after This, was his speech teacher Ida Lou Anderson's suggestion, and it turned a city into a dateline. He closed with the farewell Londoners were already saying to each other in the blackout - 'Good night, and good luck'. On the roof of Broadcasting House he described the flags: 'No one ordered these people to put out the flags... No one told them to do it, and no flag up there was white.' Millions of Americans spent the autumn of 1940 in a city they had never visited, listening. The reply came later, at a dinner in December 1941. The Librarian of Congress, Archibald MacLeish, told Murrow what the broadcasts had done: 'You laid the dead of London at our doors and we knew that the dead were our dead, were mankind's dead. You have destroyed the superstition that what is done beyond 3,000 miles of water is not really done at all.' Nothing in the exchange was private; everything in it was personal. That is the whole subject of this site, worked out on a London rooftop, overnight radio, with the sky doing the sound effects.

1947–1960 · Broadcast & Film

Close ×

Say, kids, what time is it?

The first television character to be answered by name. Children three to eight shouted its name back at the screen every afternoon for thirteen years, and the puppet it was played by was recorded before the broadcast.

The template for every children's presenter since, and the purest mechanism on this site: a figure that talks to you, built by somebody else, delivered from tape. Buffalo Bob Smith first performed Howdy Doody as a radio voice; Frank Paris built a puppet to match it; when Paris left in 1948 over merchandising rights he took the original puppet with him and the replacement debuted that June. For thirteen years and some 2,500 episodes the show opened on the same transaction - 'Say, kids, what time is it?' answered, in unison, 'It's Howdy Doody time!' - which is a named individual greeted daily by name by a room of children who could not have told you who was operating him, since the voice was usually recorded before the show. Two details do more work than the format. Clarabell the Clown never spoke for twelve years, communicating with a horn and a seltzer bottle, and said his first and only line in the final episode: 'Good-bye, kids.' A silent character choosing to speak, once, at the end. And the puppet left the screen: Howdy Doody marionettes with sliding eyes and moving mouths were sold as toys throughout the 1950s, so the relationship moved from a thing you cannot touch to an object in your hands. That is the whole thesis of this site in one commercial decision, and it was made before most of the people reading it were born.

1948 · Broadcast & Film

Close ×

Candid Camera and the unguarded face

Candid Camera put ordinary people on television without their knowledge and made the hidden reaction the show.

The format is surveillance as comedy. The audience watches a real person discover a staged situation, and the pleasure is in the unguarded face. The person is not a character and has not consented to the performance, which makes the viewer's intimacy with them one-sided in a particularly literal way.

Candid Camera is the ancestor of reality television: the ordinary person becomes the figure, and the camera's hidden position is the promise of access. The show's ethical defence was that the joke was harmless; the structural fact is that the audience is invited to enjoy a person who cannot see them.

American Bandstand and the audience on camera

American Bandstand put teenagers, records and a clean-cut host on national television every weekday, and made the audience part of the show.

Bandstand's innovation was to show the audience dancing, not just the star. A teenager at home could watch other teenagers in the studio and imagine being among them. Dick Clark's persona was friendly and non-threatening, and the music was introduced as something the audience already owned. The show is the bridge between radio fandom and the televised pop audience.

The camera made the fan visible. To watch Bandstand was to see a room of people like yourself, which turned taste into a collective identity. The star was still at the centre, but the audience was the evidence that the attachment was normal.

Rear Window and the chair by the window

Hitchcock's Rear Window puts the audience in a wheelchair with a photographer who watches his neighbours through a lens and builds a story from what he sees.

The film is a machine for making the viewer complicit in voyeurism. Jefferies cannot leave the apartment, so the window becomes his screen, and the audience shares his stolen view. The neighbours are characters because he watches them, not because he knows them.

Rear Window is the definitive cinematic statement of the one-sided gaze: the watcher is trapped, the watched cannot see him, and the plot is the consequence of his projection. The audience is in the same chair.

1956 · Broadcast & Film

Close ×

Horton and Wohl name the parasocial relationship

In 1956, Donald Horton and R. Richard Wohl published an account of the 'para-social relationship' between television viewers and the personalities who addressed them.

Horton and Wohl's contribution was to describe a structure rather than a pathology. The viewer is invited into a conversation with a performer who speaks to the camera as if to one person, and the viewer responds with the ordinary expectations of a relationship - attention, loyalty, a sense of knowing. The relationship is one-sided by design, not by failure.

They called it a 'simulacrum of conversational give and take'. The phrase is exact: the give and take is simulated on the performer's side, and the viewer's side is real. Almost every later argument about parasociality - whether it is healthy, exploitative, or simply a name for what audiences have always done - is a disagreement about which side of that sentence carries the weight.

1959 · Broadcast & Film

Close ×

The quiz show that was a performance

The Twenty-One quiz scandal exposed that the charismatic contestants Americans watched in their homes were being coached and scripted.

The quiz show gave the audience a new kind of intimate figure: an ordinary person with a face, a story and a weekly appointment. Charles Van Doren was the ideal: handsome, articulate, apparently brilliant. When the coaching was exposed, the betrayal was not only that the answers were fixed; it was that the person the audience thought they knew was a production.

The scandal is the first modern crisis of mediated authenticity. The audience had been invited to admire a contestant's mind and character, and both turned out to be written. The form survived; the trust did not. Every later reality show inherits the question the quiz scandals made unavoidable: is this person being themselves, or are they being produced?

1960 · Politics & News

Close ×

The debate that was won by the picture

On 26 September 1960, John F. Kennedy and Richard Nixon met in the first televised presidential debate; the same broadcast was heard by radio listeners and seen by television viewers.

The often-repeated finding is that radio listeners thought Nixon had won and television viewers thought Kennedy had. The polls behind that claim are less tidy than the anecdote, but the structural point survives: the same words, delivered through two media, produced two different candidates. Television added a face, a posture and a reaction shot to a contest that had been conducted through voice and print.

The debate made the body part of the argument. A viewer could compare the two men's ease, sweat and gaze in real time, and could feel addressed by a candidate who looked into the lens. The intimacy of that look is borrowed: the candidate is speaking to millions, and each viewer receives it as a private appeal.

1964 · Music & Fan Culture

Close ×

Beatlemania: the scream as a mass reply

The Beatles arrived at New York's JFK airport on 7 February 1964 and appeared on The Ed Sullivan Show two days later before an audience of tens of millions.

Beatlemania is often described as hysteria, which explains nothing. The scream was a structured response: it was collective, it was timed to the appearance, and it functioned as a way of participating in an event that offered no other participation. The performers could not hear the audience; the audience could see and hear the performers. The asymmetry was the point.

The screaming also made the music secondary. Fans were not mainly listening; they were being in the same room as the image, and the image was on a screen or a stage. The industrial apparatus - records, television, merchandise, airport arrivals - arranged the proximity. What looked like loss of control was an efficient way of producing intimacy at scale.

1966 · Digital & Synthetic

Close ×

ELIZA and the feeling of being understood

A short pattern-matching script that reflects the user's words back with questions attached. Most people told it they understood, within minutes.

The founding demonstration that an attentive-seeming system is enough, and that the belief is generated by the response rather than by the intelligence behind it. Every companion app since is a bigger ELIZA, and the field has still not fully absorbed what that first one proved.

The script had no model of the user and no memory of the conversation; it reflected the last sentence back as a question. The users who confided in it were not fooled by its intelligence, because there was none. They were caught by the shape of the reply, which is the whole of the ELIZA effect.

Star Trek and the fandom that outlived the show

Star Trek's cancellation did not end the relationship: fans wrote letters, organised conventions and kept the characters alive after the show left the air.

Star Trek is the first television fandom to treat a cancelled show as a continuing world. Fans wrote to the studio, produced fanzines and met at conventions; the characters existed in a shared future that the audience could inhabit. The bond was with a crew as much as with a star, which made the fandom a community rather than a crowd.

The letter-writing campaign is the key evidence. It treated a scheduling decision as a personal loss and a public cause, which is the moment a fan audience begins to act like a constituency.

1969 · Music & Fan Culture

Close ×

Manson hears the White Album as an instruction

Charles Manson read The Beatles' White Album as a coded message about an apocalyptic race war and directed his followers to commit murder.

Manson's relationship to the album was a fan's relationship taken to its extreme: he treated a mass-produced text as a personal instruction. The songs were not addressed to him, but he heard them as addressed to him, and he built a cosmology around the coincidence. The victims were chosen to trigger the war he believed the album predicted.

The case is not an argument that music causes violence. It is an argument that a text can be read as a private message by someone who needs it to be one. The far end - the Beatles, the album, the culture - had no knowledge of Manson, and that ignorance is what made the interpretation possible.

1970s–1980s · Politics & News
