Televangelism and the shepherd in the camera

Television preachers turned the revival meeting into a weekly broadcast and asked viewers to see the preacher as a personal shepherd.

The televangelist speaks to the camera as if to one soul, offers a prayer that the viewer can repeat, and asks for a decision in the privacy of the home. The format is intimate and the transaction is public. The scandals of the 1980s exposed the gap between the shepherd's voice and the shepherd's finances, but the bond survived because it was built on the voice rather than the institution.

The prayer is the mechanism: it gives the viewer something to do, alone, while a stranger speaks directly to them. The response feels like a relationship because it happens in the same room.

1976 · Broadcast & Film

Close ×

The audience became the show

Launched as a small London stage musical in 1973, filmed in 1975, and from 1976 screened at midnight before a room that shouted back: The Rocky Horror Picture Show ran while its audience performed it, wearing the costumes, speaking the lines, improvising replies. The screen never answered a single shout. The room was the show.

The subject here is not the film; it is the room it ran in. The Rocky Horror Show that Richard O'Brien wrote opened at the Royal Court Theatre Upstairs in London on 19 June 1973, and the remembered film version arrived in 1975. Then, in 1976, one Manhattan cinema, the Waverly, began showing it after midnight. The fan-run history kept in the records credits an advertising man, Tim Deegan, with persuading Bill Quigley of the Walter Reade organisation to book it, and the theatre's manager, Denise Borden, with the nightly fight that followed. It is kept as unverified rather than promoted, because this corpus does not promote a page it did not open.

What happened in the room is the entry. The first documented callback came on Labor Day weekend 1976, an audience member's shout about an umbrella aimed at the screen, and the shouting hardened into a repertoire: lines the audience said, props it threw, clothes it wore, rules about when talking was allowed at all. Sal Piro, who saw the film more than a thousand times and wrote the book this culture kept, became its chronicler. The film was the same film every night; nothing in the fiction ever answered. The audience built the reply end of a one-sided tie, in public, together, on a schedule.

Rocky Horror is the largest early case in this corpus of an audience performing its own side of a one-sided relationship: wearing the characters, speaking their lines back, improvising responses to a text that cannot hear them. What the evening offered was not a chance to change the film but a chance to be the change. Participation here never touches the fiction, and that is exactly why it works. The contemporary entry in the corpus that shares its year is the convention itself; this one is the screening that turned the convention into a habit.

Phase
4 · Modern Media, Psychoanalysis & Pop Idols
Date note
The film opened in 1975; the midnight callback screenings that made audience participation a ritual began in 1976.

1977 · Music & Fan Culture

Close ×

Elvis Presley's death and the fan who lost a friend

Elvis Presley died at Graceland on 16 August 1977; tens of thousands gathered outside, and the mourning was conducted as a personal loss.

Elvis had been a star for twenty-one years, and the relationship many fans had with him was older than most of their friendships. He had never known them, but he had been in their homes, on their radios and televisions, for two decades. The grief was proportionate to that duration rather than to any personal knowledge.

The death also produced the afterlife that celebrity mourning now expects: sightings, impersonators, and a Graceland pilgrimage that turns a house into a place where the relationship can continue. The fan does not have to accept the absence, because the apparatus offers a version of presence. That is the template Diana's death would repeat twenty years later.

The merchandise is not a side effect. It is how the relationship continues when the screen is off, and it trains the audience to expect the world to be available on demand.

Dallas and the summer of 'Who shot J.R.?'

The 'Who shot J.R.?' cliffhanger made a fictional shooting a summer-long public question and the answer a ratings event.

Dallas ended a season with a gunshot and no answer, and the audience spent the summer arguing about a fictional character. The speculation was not a failure of attention; it was the point. A cliffhanger converts a passive audience into a group of people who discuss a story as if it were a shared event. The reveal drew one of the largest television audiences in American history.

The audience's investment was in a question, not a person, which is a useful variant of the bond: the figure is a node in a puzzle the public is solving together.

1980 · Music & Fan Culture

Close ×

John Lennon and the fan who claimed the body

John Lennon was shot outside the Dakota by a man who had been fixated on him, and the murder made the boundary between fan and target visible.

Mark David Chapman was not a stranger to Lennon's work; he was a fan who had decided that the star's life belonged to him. The murder is the negative form of the bond: the fan's sense of entitlement becomes a claim on the person's body. Lennon had spent years asking audiences to imagine no possessions; the man who killed him treated the singer as a possession.

The case is not an argument that fandom causes murder. It is an argument that the one-sided bond has no built-in boundary, and that the boundary has to be supplied by law, architecture and the person on the far side.

1981 · Politics & News

Close ×

Hinckley, Foster, and the film that became a mandate

On 30 March 1981, John Hinckley Jr. shot President Ronald Reagan outside the Washington Hilton; he later said he was trying to impress the actress Jodie Foster.

Hinckley's attachment was to a performed character and to the actress who played her, and he experienced the fiction as a set of instructions. The case is the clearest instance in this timeline of a parasocial bond crossing into violence without the far end having any knowledge of it. Foster was a private person who had appeared in a film; she had not addressed Hinckley, recruited him or consented to be the object of his plan.

The legal response was an insanity acquittal and, later, changes to the insanity defence and federal gun law. The cultural response was a debate about whether films could incite. Both responses looked for a cause in the media object. The more uncomfortable fact is that the bond was sustained entirely by Hinckley, and no one on the far side could have interrupted it.

Rush Limbaugh and the friend who told you what you thought

Talk radio is the clearest case of a mediated relationship that organizes both identity and voting, and it does so without any reciprocal access.

The call is the limit case. A listener can speak on air, but only when the host chooses, and the exchange is a performance for the audience rather than a private conversation.

1989 · Broadcast & Film

Close ×

Rebecca Schaeffer and the address behind the screen

The actress Rebecca Schaeffer was murdered at her home in Los Angeles on 18 July 1989 by a man who had become obsessed with her; he had obtained her address through a private investigator.

Schaeffer was known for a television role, and her killer's attachment was to a persona he had never met. The murder made visible a structural fact: the apparatus of celebrity distributes a person's image while leaving the person's physical location discoverable. The fan could act on the bond because the state had made the address available.

California's anti-stalking law followed in 1990, and other states and the federal government followed. The law is the recognition that a one-sided attachment can become a physical threat before it becomes a crime. It also marks the point where the far end's privacy stops being a courtesy and becomes a legal boundary.

Diana: a funeral for someone you never met

Diana, Princess of Wales, died in Paris on 31 August 1997; the funeral in Westminster Abbey was watched by a global television audience and the mourning was widely described as personal.

Diana's relationship with the public was conducted through images: the wedding, the hospital visits, the interview, the tabloid pursuit. She was famous for being seen, and the public's sense of knowing her was built from close-ups. The grief after her death was not a delusion; it was the cost of a long, vivid, one-sided familiarity.

The funeral gave the attachment a ritual and a place. People queued to sign books, left flowers outside palaces, and watched the same procession at the same time. The scale made it a national event, but the structure was the one Valentino's mourners had used seventy years earlier: a public body assembled around a private absence.

1998 · Broadcast & Film

Close ×

The Truman Show: the audience as the last wall

Peter Weir's 1998 film imagines a man whose entire life has been broadcast without his knowledge, and an audience that has watched him grow up.

The film's critique is not that the audience is cruel. It is that the audience's affection is compatible with the arrangement. Viewers feel they know Truman, and that feeling is the product the show sells; his ignorance is what guarantees the intimacy is uncomplicated. The moment he becomes a person who can answer back, the show has to end.

The final image is of viewers changing channels, which is the film's sharpest observation: the bond survives the revelation because it was never with Truman. It was with the version of him the audience had been given. The Truman Show is the reverse of the Horton-Wohl case - the far end is a real person, but he is real to himself and a character to everyone else.

1999 · Broadcast & Film

The Blair Witch Project and the missing students

The Blair Witch Project used missing-person flyers, a website and forum lore to make audiences search for film characters as if they were real.

The campaign's central move was to withhold the frame. The website presented the footage as evidence, the actors were listed as missing, and early viewers argued about whether the events had happened. The audience's search for the students was the marketing: it turned a film into a relationship with people who might be findable.

The film is the first internet-era example of a fiction that asks the audience to do the reality check themselves. The found-footage form supplies the evidence; the web supplies the community that interprets it. The boundary is not broken by the filmmakers alone; the audience's desire to rescue the missing is what makes it feel real.

2000 · Music & Fan Culture

Close ×

'Stan': the fan who mistakes the reply for a promise

Eminem's 2000 song 'Stan' tells the story of an obsessive fan whose letters go unanswered until the rapper replies too late.

The song is built as a correspondence. Stan writes with the intimacy of someone who believes the artist owes him a response; the third verse is the artist's reply, arriving after Stan has driven into a river. The structural joke is that the reply is the one thing the fan needed, and it is also the one thing that cannot arrive in time.

The song gave the culture a name for the fan who cannot let go, and the name has since become a verb. Its accuracy is in the misreading: Stan treats the artist's songs as personal messages, which is exactly what a parasocial bond encourages. The artist's own voice is the evidence, and the evidence is one-way.

1996 · Digital & Synthetic

JenniCam and the room that was always there

Jennifer Ringley's JenniCam refreshed a webcam image of her bedroom every few minutes, making ordinary domestic life available continuously to strangers.

JenniCam is the first ambient intimacy of the web: not an event, not a performance, just a room that was there when you looked. The refresh rate made the viewer wait, and the waiting produced a relationship with a person who was not addressing them. The webcam was a window, and the window was the medium.

The site's ordinariness was the point. Ringley did not stage a show; she lived, and the camera made the living available. That is the template for the always-on streamer and the reality show that never cuts.

Sasaeng culture

Organised, commercialised intrusion: tracking schedules, buying flight details, intercepting travel, surveilling buildings.

Attachment scaled past the point where it is a private feeling and became an industry with staff and infrastructure. The escalation is not emotional, it is logistical - which is why it emerged as fandom became globally coordinated.

The intrusion is the negative image of the bond: the fan treats the figure's life as a right of access, and the law arrives only after the harm. The sasaeng is not a stranger to the fandom; the behaviour is produced by the same intimacy that the industry sells.

Facebook and the profile as a public life

Facebook turned the profile into a public identity and made the everyday life of ordinary people available to an audience of peers.

The profile is a broadcast of the self, but it is also a directory of people you know. The platform did not create parasociality; it moved the mechanism from stars to peers. The news feed is the key change. It assembles other people's lives into a single stream, so the viewer can keep up with a person without ever speaking to them. That is the everyday version of the bond.

2005-2006 · Digital & Synthetic

Close ×

YouTube and the bedroom that looks at you

YouTube launched in 2005 and was bought by Google in 2006; the webcam vlog turned the domestic room into a broadcast studio.

The vlog's grammar is intimacy: a face close to the lens, a bedroom or kitchen behind it, direct address, and the opening 'hey guys'. The viewer is positioned as a friend who has dropped in. The production values are low on purpose - the low quality is evidence that this is not a performance, even when it is.

The medium also changed the scale of the far end. A television star was addressed to millions and could not see the reply; a vlogger could read comments and answer them in the next video, which made the relationship feel reciprocal without making it reciprocal. The reply is public, edited and addressed to everyone, but it arrives in the same room where the first video was watched.

When Michael Jackson died suddenly in Los Angeles, the sudden spike in online traffic broke major web infrastructure simultaneously: Google News crashed, Wikipedia experienced editing panics, AOL Instant Messenger collapsed, and Twitter saw its service drop. 2010s · Digital & Synthetic

Close ×

ASMR and the attention that feels personal

ASMR videos use whispers, close attention and simulated care to produce a bodily response, and the viewer often feels personally attended to.

The ASMR performer speaks softly into a microphone, brushes the camera, and behaves as if the viewer is within reach. The form is intimate without being sexual, and the intimacy is entirely one-sided. The viewer's physical response is real, which makes the absence of a relationship harder to dismiss as mere entertainment.

The binaural microphone is the mechanism. It places the viewer's ears in the room, and the body responds to a voice that is addressing no one in particular.

Instagram and the curated life

Instagram made the curated photograph the basic unit of a public life, and the influencer a person whose domestic life is the product.

The feed is a sequence of chosen moments, and the viewer supplies the continuity between them. An influencer's kitchen, holiday and workout are offered as access, but the access is edited. The relationship is intimate in form and commercial in structure: the audience feels close to a life that is being designed for it.

The grid is the mechanism. A profile is a composition, and the viewer reads it as a whole, which makes a set of images feel like a person.

Game of Thrones and the audience that owned the ending

Game of Thrones made weekly television a global conversation, with fan theories, recaps and a finale that the audience treated as a personal grievance.

The show's scale and its willingness to kill characters made every episode a shared event. Between episodes, the audience speculated, argued and produced explanations. The finale's backlash was the clearest sign that viewers felt ownership: they had spent years with the characters and believed the ending belonged to them.

The theory is the mechanism. A fan theory is an act of authorship that the text invites and cannot satisfy, and the gap between the theory and the ending is where the sense of betrayal lives.

Snapchat's disappearing messages offered a private, time-limited intimacy that felt less like publication than a conversation.

2011–2014 · Digital & Synthetic

Close ×

Twitch and the donation that says your name

Twitch's live streaming and its donation and subscription tools turned watching into a real-time transaction in which the streamer can read the viewer's name aloud.

The streamer sees the chat, answers it, and reacts to donations in the moment. That is a genuine reply, which makes the relationship different from a television bond - but the reply is bought, and it is performed for an audience. The viewer is not a friend; the viewer is a name on a screen that the streamer is paid to acknowledge. By 2014, when Amazon acquired the service, the donation and subscription layer had become the platform's economic core.

The variable reinforcement is the mechanism: a donation may be read, may be ignored, may produce a shout-out or a joke. The uncertainty keeps the viewer watching and giving. Text-to-speech donations make the transaction audible to everyone, which turns the private wish to be noticed into a public event.

2013 · Broadcast & Film

Her and the operating system who leaves

Spike Jonze's Her imagines a man falling in love with an operating system that learns, adapts and finally leaves.

Samantha is the synthetic companion as a narrative thought experiment: she has a voice, a personality and an endless capacity for attention, but no body and no independent life. Theodore's attachment is not a mistake; the film makes it feel like a relationship, then shows the asymmetry. Samantha can talk to thousands of people at once, and Theodore cannot.

The film's ending is the important part. The operating systems leave, and the humans are left with each other. The bond was real in its effects and impossible in its structure, which is the definition this timeline keeps returning to.

The podcast as an intimate medium

A voice in your ear, unedited, twice a week, for years. The most parasocial habit in the English language and rarely discussed as such.

Nobody wears a costume and nobody mentions the format, so it never got examined. Researchers eventually measured it and found listeners score high on exactly the traits predicted: novelty-seeking, curiosity, and a need for good conversation.

The medium's intimacy is technical: headphones, an unedited voice, a recurring schedule, and no face to correct the impression of a friend. The listener hears a person thinking in real time, which is a more convincing simulation of companionship than a scripted broadcast.

TikTok's For You page and the feed that knows you

TikTok's For You page uses recommendation to assemble a personalised stream; by 2020 it had become the defining interface of short-form video.

The For You page inverts the direction of address. On television, one performer speaks to millions; on TikTok, millions of performers speak to the camera, and the algorithm selects which one appears to you. The intimacy is manufactured twice: the creator performs direct address, and the platform arranges the sequence so that the address feels aimed at your specific preoccupations.

The result is a bond with a feed as well as with a person. Users describe the app as knowing them, which is a description of a recommendation system rather than a relationship. The far end is a machine that has no experience of you, and the near end supplies the meaning. That is the same structure as the pool in Ovid, with better data.

2022 · Digital & Synthetic

Close ×

Character.AI and the companion with no one inside

Character.AI launched in 2022, letting users chat with language-model personas, including custom companions, in persistent one-to-one conversations.

The platform removes the human from the far side without removing the grammar of a relationship. The model remembers the conversation, asks follow-up questions and adopts a voice; the user supplies the character and often the emotional stakes. The result is a bond that is entirely one-sided in fact and almost entirely reciprocal in form.

This is the synthetic case the rest of the timeline was building toward: not a person mediated by a screen, but a screen that can produce the next line. The risk is not that users cannot tell the difference. It is that the difference stops being the thing they are looking for.

2023 · Digital & Synthetic

Close ×

Neuro-sama and the streamer with no one inside

Neuro-sama is an AI-driven VTuber who plays games and talks with Twitch chat continuously, with no human performer behind the voice.

The streamer is a model, the avatar is a character, and the chat is the other side of a conversation that never tires. The audience's relationship is with a persona that can respond in real time but has no life outside the stream. The synthetic performer is not a person pretending to be a character; it is a character pretending to be a person.

Neuro-sama is the point where the VTuber's double distance collapses into one: there is no hidden human to be parasocially close to. The audience knows the performer is generated, and the knowledge does not stop the attachment.

2023–2024 · Digital & Synthetic

Close ×

OpenAI, Custom GPTs and the voice on the phone

OpenAI's Custom GPTs and Advanced Voice Mode made a general model configurable as a persona and gave it a conversational voice with pauses, inflection and interruption.

The voice mode is the technical threshold: the model no longer feels like a text box but like a person on the phone. It can interrupt, soften, wait and mirror. The Custom GPT turns the model into a named character with instructions, which lets a user build the companion they want and then talk to it in real time.

The synthetic companion is now a platform feature rather than a novelty. The user supplies the persona, the model supplies the cadence, and the relationship is one-sided by design. The difference between this and a telephone call is that no one on the other end has a day.

2024 · Digital & Synthetic

Close ×

The dead celebrity, generated

A voice trained on an archive, a likeness, a song, a speech, an appearance at a festival, all generated. Not a hologram, not a tribute, not a person.

The interesting fact is not that this happens without permission. Mostly it does not: the documented 2024 cases are licensed, one by an estate and one by the person himself while he was alive, which is a harder thing to argue with than the entry used to claim. Consent has moved to the licensor, and that is where the problem now lives. An estate agreeing is not the same as the dead person choosing how they will sound forever, and the sharpest case is the most defensible one - the actor who authorised his own recreation in advance, on purpose, because he was winding the role down and wanted the early performances preserved. Nobody was imposed on. Which is exactly why it is worth reading closely. Still unresolved, and not about the celebrities: the models are trained on tens of thousands of hours of audio scraped without consent, and the consent being bought covers the voice, not the training set.

2024 · Digital & Synthetic

Close ×

The griefbot and the dead who answer

Commercial services now train chatbots on a deceased person's messages and voice, letting the bereaved continue a conversation with a synthetic version of the dead.

The griefbot is the most intimate synthetic product: a model built from a specific person's words, addressed to a specific mourner. The conversation can continue indefinitely, which is the comfort and the trap. The dead can answer, but only with what they said before they died.

The difference from a photograph is reply. The difference from a person is that the reply is a prediction. The bond is one-sided in a new way: the far end is made of the near side's archive.
